title: 67 Original Sound
blurb: The hook that started everything: five seconds of Skrilla's 'Doot Doot (6 7)', the exact cut that basketball editors laid over LaMelo Ball highlights until two numbers became a worldwide chant. This is the sound teachers now dread, preserved at the source. Everything else on the 67 shelf is a remix, a parody or a descendant of what you can hear here. Drop it into a call and someone will answer 'seven' before they realise what they have done. The reflex is the whole meme, and this clip is what installed it.
origin: The hook from Skrilla's 'Doot Doot (6 7)', the track behind the 67 meme.

title: 67 Full Song
blurb: Skrilla's 'Doot Doot (6 7)' existed before the meme did: a Philadelphia drill track that first surfaced in December 2024, months ahead of the basketball edits that carried its hook into classrooms on several continents. This longer cut gives the chant some room to breathe — nearly twenty seconds of it rather than the usual sting. Useful when a quick 'six seven' won't do and the moment calls for full immersion. Play it for anyone who insists they don't know the song; their face will confirm otherwise within about four seconds.
origin: An extended cut of Skrilla's 'Doot Doot (6 7)' (2024), the source of the 67 chant.

title: 6 7 Sound Effect
blurb: Editors needed a clean version of the six-seven sting, and this is it: the chant clipped tight, no intro, no tail, ready to land on a punchline. The 67 meme spread as much through edits as through classrooms, and a usable sound effect is the unglamorous infrastructure underneath all of it. Five seconds, in and out. Stack it over a basketball highlight, a test score, a receipt totalling £6.70, or anything else the numbers can be tortured into. No setup required, and that is most of the reason it conquered the planet.
origin: A clean edit-ready cut of the six-seven hook from Skrilla's 'Doot Doot (6 7)'.

title: 67 Kid
blurb: March 2025, a Cam Wilder basketball video, and one blonde kid in the crowd yelling 'six seven' with his hands out in the meme's signature palms-up bounce — that clip minted the 67 Kid, the movement's unofficial mascot. The internet promptly christened him 'Mason', invented a whole personality type around him, and remixed his moment into oblivion. He did not create the chant; Skrilla's track did. He is simply the person who performed it hardest. Eleven seconds of total commitment, useful whenever enthusiasm outruns dignity.
origin: The kid filmed chanting 'six seven' at a Cam Wilder basketball video in March 2025.

title: 67 Mini Version
blurb: Two seconds flat. The mini version of the 67 chant exists for moments when timing matters more than volume: the beat of silence after a question, the split second before a teacher regains control, the gap between a friend saying 'six' and everyone else in the call joining in. Brainrot audio tends to sprawl, so a properly trimmed cut is rarer than it should be. Keep this one loaded for rapid-fire responses. The full-length versions are for ceremony; this is for combat.
origin: A trimmed two-second cut of the 67 chant.

title: 67 Aura Edition
blurb: Aura, in current internet usage, is the invisible points system by which coolness is won and lost, and bolting it onto 67 was inevitable: two pieces of Gen Alpha vocabulary fused into one eighteen-second remix. The Aura Edition treats the chant the way edit culture treats everything, as raw material for something more dramatic than the source ever asked to be. Use it to award aura, to revoke it, or to score any act of unearned confidence. Nobody involved can define either term, and nobody needs to.
origin: A remix of the 67 chant circulated as the 'Aura Edition'.

title: I Am a Baby 67
blurb: Somewhere below the age of forming full sentences, the 67 meme found its youngest demographic. 'I'm a baby... six seven' became a TikTok fixture through videos of toddlers being inducted into the chant long before they could possibly understand it, proof of how far down the age range this thing burrowed. Nine seconds of it live here. Parents use it on their own children, older siblings use it as an accusation, and everyone else uses it to declare themselves too small and too innocent to be blamed for anything.
origin: From TikTok's 'I'm a baby, 67' trend of toddler six-seven videos.

title: 67 Brain Fart
blurb: A brain fart is what happens when your head simply stops serving the file you asked for, and this clip is that experience with a number attached. It belongs to the late, degraded stage of the 67 cycle, when the chant had been remixed so many times that coherence stopped being the point. Twelve seconds of a thought failing in real time. Play it when someone forgets the word they were reaching for, blanks on a name mid-introduction, or answers an easy question with the only two digits their brain still stocks.
origin: A '67 brain fart' remix clip circulated on meme soundboards.

title: 67 on a Merry Rizzmas
blurb: Christmas 2025 got its own brainrot carol. TikToker @html.brainrot set the season's entire slang inventory to the tune of We Wish You a Merry Christmas, and '67 on a merry rizzmas' was the line that stuck, powering a lip-dub and dance trend built around the 67 hand gesture and an aggressively held rizz face. The original sound racked up tens of thousands of uses within a fortnight of appearing in mid-November. This is the seasonal branch of the 67 family tree: play it from December 1st, retire it by Boxing Day, repeat annually.
origin: From '67 Rizzmas' by TikToker @html.brainrot (November 2025), set to We Wish You a Merry Christmas.

title: 789 Meme
blurb: Why was six afraid of seven? Because seven eight nine: a joke old enough that your grandparents groaned at it, resurrected by a generation that turned two of those numbers into a religion. Once 67 had saturated every classroom, 789 was sitting right there as the obvious next move, and TikTok duly moved. This twenty-second clip carries the gag in its modern meme form. It works as a follow-up whenever the six-seven call-and-response has run its course, and as a peace offering between generations, since it is the one number joke everyone in the room already knows.
origin: The 'seven eight nine' number joke in its TikTok-era meme form.

title: 9 Plus 10 Vine
blurb: Ancient history by internet standards: 2013, the Vine era, a kid asked what nine plus ten is, and the immortal answer, twenty-one. Every number-based chant that Gen Alpha now torments teachers with is descended from this six-second exchange, delivered with a certainty that no correct answer has ever matched. The 67 crowd rediscovered it as a sort of founding document and put it back into rotation a decade on. Play it beside the modern stuff and the family resemblance is unmistakable: confidence first, arithmetic never.
origin: The 2013 'what's 9 plus 10' Vine.

title: Take the L
blurb: Losing in Fortnite was never allowed to be private. The Take the L emote arrived in the 2018 battle pass and instantly became the game's premier act of disrespect: an L pressed to the forehead, legs kicking through a jaunty little dance, performed over your body while you watch from spectate. Victory royales are forgotten in minutes; being Take the L'd is carried for life. The sound alone now does the work of the whole animation, deployed in edits and Discord calls wherever somebody has lost in a manner worth commemorating.
origin: The Take the L emote from Fortnite's 2018 battle pass.

title: 19 Dollar Fortnite Card
blurb: 'Nineteen dollar Fortnite card. Who wants it?' In January 2021 a TikToker called @mrblocku filmed himself in a car seat frantically waving a V-Bucks card at the camera, and the internet decided this was cinema. The choppy recording, the sped-up delivery and the total absence of context made it irresistible remix material; one popular edit bolted on PlayStation sound effects and a squeaky voice announcing 'no more Fortnite'. Half a decade later it remains the standard audio for any suspicious act of generosity. Accept nothing from anyone while this is playing.
origin: From @mrblocku's January 2021 TikTok waving a $19 Fortnite V-Bucks card.

title: Coral Chorus
blurb: Deep in the Chapter 1 Season 8 battle pass, at tier 54, sat a lobby music pack called Coral Chorus, and anyone who played Fortnite in 2019 has absorbed it whether they wanted to or not. Lobby music occupies a strange place in gaming memory — you never chose to listen, yet it soundtracked thousands of hours of waiting for the bus. That is exactly the nostalgia this track now trades on, complete with ten-hour YouTube loops and meme remixes. Play it near a lapsed Fortnite player and watch 2019 happen to them in real time.
origin: The Coral Chorus lobby music from Fortnite's Chapter 1 Season 8 battle pass (2019).

title: Among Us Series Intro
blurb: Among Us became a television show, which still sounds like a joke until you check the cast list. The animated series arrived on Paramount+ in 2025 from Owen Dennis, the creator of Infinity Train, with Dan Stevens, Patton Oswalt and Wayne Knight in the voice cast. This intro is the sound of a lobby game about lying to your friends being taken seriously as drama, and it was always going to end up on soundboards. Use it to open anything with more ceremony than it deserves: a group call, a study session, a round of the actual game.
origin: The intro from the Among Us animated series (Paramount+, 2025).

title: Oh Wowie Wawa
blurb: Nonsense syllables, two seconds of them, attached forever to a green Among Us character and repeated across more edits than anyone could count. 'Oh wowie wawa' means nothing in any language, and communities in at least three of them have gone looking anyway; the hunt for a translation became part of the joke. It spread the way the best meme audio spreads, as a rhythmic noise that is easier to repeat than to explain. Reach for it as an all-purpose reaction to surprise, delight, or mild concussion, whichever the moment supplies.
origin: A nonsense vocal line popularised through Among Us edits.

title: Guy Yelling Among Us
blurb: Under one second long, and somehow it says everything: a man bellowing the name of the game with the urgency of someone reporting a fire. Brevity is the entire utility here. The clip ends before anyone can react, making it the ideal interruption — no build-up, no aftermath, just a sudden and complete derailment of whatever was being discussed. Soundboard veterans know that the shortest clips get the most use, and this one approaches the theoretical minimum. Spam responsibly, or at least spam with a sense of rhythm.
origin: A short clip of a man yelling 'Among Us'.

title: When the Imposter Is Sus
blurb: In November 2020 a Jerma985 fan ran the streamer's face through FaceApp, produced a smile no human face should hold, and posted it to Reddit. A Discord user captioned it 'When the impostor is sus!' and one of the most disturbing images of the Among Us era was complete. The audio treatment followed: fourteen slow seconds built to accompany that unblinking zoom, equal parts comedy and threat. It peaked in March 2021 and never fully left. Play it when someone in the call has gone suspiciously quiet, and let the silence do the accusing.
origin: Audio from the 'When the Impostor Is Sus' Jerma985 meme (2020).

title: FaceTime Call
blurb: No sound on earth makes a room check its phones faster. The FaceTime ring is Apple's most theatrical piece of audio design, a rolling chime that repeats with rising social pressure until somebody answers, and it has become the backbone of an entire genre of prank: play it near any iPhone owner and watch the scramble. Editors lean on it just as hard, since nothing establishes 'an important call is happening' more economically. It sits alongside the connect chirp and the hang-up as the trilogy's dramatic opening act — the part where you could still choose not to answer.
origin: Apple's FaceTime ringtone.

title: Squid Game Theme
blurb: Jung Jae-il, the composer behind Parasite's score, gave Squid Game music that works by wrong-footing you: childlike, almost playful instrumentation carrying a show about debt and death. That tension is the reason the soundtrack escaped Netflix and colonised TikTok within weeks of the 2021 premiere, scoring everything from faithful gameplay recreations to people deciding between two snacks. This twenty-five second cut is the recognisable heart of it. One bar is enough to put viewers back in the arena, braced for elimination over something as minor as picking the wrong queue at a supermarket.
origin: Theme music from Netflix's Squid Game (2021), scored by Jung Jae-il.

title: Squid Game S2
blurb: Season two arrived on Netflix in December 2024 and immediately handed the internet a new obsession: the Mingle game, a rotating carousel, a sweetly sung round-and-round nursery tune, and a purple-haired maniac called Thanos dancing through all of it. TikTok ran the song into the ground by early January. This nine-second clip bottles that second-season sound for soundboard use, and it slots neatly into the role the doll's song played in 2021: pleasant noise, terrible implications. Play it while people are choosing teams for anything at all and enjoy the flicker of panic.
origin: From Squid Game season 2 (Netflix, December 2024).
